Hello Space Apps community!  We are AC DC. We’ve gathered for this hackathon to tackle the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. 

Team status: We already have a complete team. Good luck to everyone!
summary: Free Return: Junior Astronaut Trainer is a NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 project from team AC DC, built to answer the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.” It is a pixel-art space game made in JavaScript and HTML, in which the player works as a technician preparing a rocket and a flight from launch to splashdown across four missions: launch preparation, flight to the Moon, moonwalk, and the return to Earth. The project uses real NASA data, including solar flares from DONKI, storms from EONET, research from OSDR, launch weather from POWER, Moon terrain from LRO LOLA, and Earth images from GIBS and EPIC. The source code is in the repository github.com/Kokusabo/Junior_astronaut_trainer.
details:
What it does. A pixel-art browser game that teaches kids how a Moon trip really works, in four missions. You prepare a rocket on the pad, fly to the Moon (launch, the burn, a three-day flight, the landing), explore on three moonwalks, then lift off, dock, and come home through the air with a heat shield and parachutes. Fuel, stars and cargo carry from one mission to the next, so one trip is one story. An optional tutorial and five practice drills teach every skill.
Real NASA data. Launch weather (NASA POWER) decides GO and NO-GO days. Solar flares (DONKI), storms (EONET) and a real asteroid flyby (JPL) become in-game events. JPL Horizons gives the Earth-Moon distance. The Earth is drawn from GIBS maps and an EPIC photo, and the Moon terrain you land on is built from LRO LOLA elevation data. NASA OSDR studies provide facts.
Impact. Players learn by doing: the gravity turn, burn windows, slow docking and the narrow re-entry angle. Mistakes cost stars but never end a mission, and it works with keyboard or touch.
Tools. Plain HTML, JavaScript and CSS on a canvas, with no libraries or build step. It runs offline from a folder, with saved copies of the data, and the rules are tested in Node. Pixel art and sound are generated in code.
Use of AI. Claude (Anthropic) wrote the code, tests, text and pixel-art code. Every scene shows an "AI-GENERATED ART (CLAUDE)" mark, and the footers, meta tags and README say so too. No NASA logos, flags or mission patches are used.
